state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain to me why you combined 2n and (2m+1) in that way? What do you think the term 2n represents in this context?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought 2n was just a number, like any other number, so I could just add it to (2m + 1). I didn't really think about what 2n actually means. Does it always have to be even, or can it be something else? I'm a bit confused about that.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any examples where 2n might represent an odd number? Let's explore different scenarios to see if we can come to a conclusion about what 2n typically represents in mathematics.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess I can't think of any examples where 2n would be odd because if n is a whole number, then 2n would always be even, right? But I'm still not sure why that is. Like, what if n was something weird? Does it still have to be even?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the 2n misconception through targeted questioning that prompts the student to reason about why 2n must be even, leading to visible progress as the student moves from uncertainty to recognizing that 2n is always even for whole numbers, though some residual confusion remains about edge cases.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking (asking about why they combined terms, what 2n represents, and requesting counterexamples), never provides direct answers, and successfully prompts the student to discover that 2n is always even through their own reasoning.
